title: How Seq2Seq reads a sentence into a vector, writes a translation, and beats statistical MT
summary: Seq2Seq uses one LSTM to read a sentence into an 8,000-dimensional vector and another LSTM to write the translation, beating statistical machine translation for the first time at scale. We unpack the encoder-decoder, why reversed input helps, where the 384M parameters go, and how beam search works, then follow the fixed-length bottleneck to attention.
ai_summary: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks (Google, 2014) uses a 4-layer LSTM to encode the input sentence into a fixed-length vector, then another 4-layer LSTM to generate the translation word by word. On WMT'14 English-to-French, a 5-model ensemble translates directly to BLEU 34.81, beating the phrase-based SMT baseline's 33.30; rescoring the SMT system's 1,000 candidates reaches 36.5. Reversing the source sentence lifts a single model from BLEU 25.9 to 30.6, which the authors attribute to shortening the minimal distance between corresponding words. Its main limitation: all information has to fit into one fixed-length vector.
brief: Problem: Neural networks could only handle fixed-size inputs and outputs, so there was no general solution for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation.
Method: An encoder LSTM reads the whole sentence into one vector, and a decoder LSTM generates the translation word by word. Four layers, two separate LSTMs, and reversed source input.

Result: A 5-model ensemble reaches BLEU 34.81 and becomes the first pure neural translation system to beat statistical machine translation at scale; rescoring reaches 36.5, and long sentences don't fall apart.

Limitations: The whole sentence is squeezed into a fixed-length vector, the vocabulary is limited, and word-by-word computation is hard to parallelize. Attention, subword segmentation, and Transformers later solve these problems.

paper.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
paper.authors: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, Quoc V. Le

cover.headline: A close reading of the Seq2Seq paper
cover.highlight: Read it into a vector, then write the translation

sections.h: The conclusion first: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In September 2014, Google's Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc V. Le released this paper, only nine pages long. It proposed a structure that now seems entirely natural: **use one neural network to “read” a sentence into a vector, then another neural network to “write” that vector into another sentence**. This is sequence-to-sequence learning, or Seq2Seq, also called the encoder-decoder architecture.

On English-to-French translation, with almost no linguistic knowledge built in, this model became the first to clearly outperform a traditional phrase-based statistical machine translation system at scale (BLEU 34.8 vs. 33.3). Used to rescore 1,000 candidates from the conventional system, it reached BLEU 36.5, just 0.5 below the best result at the time of 37.0.

The paper also has a surprising small trick: **reverse the source sentence**. Translation quality improves sharply: BLEU jumps from 25.9 to 30.6. The logic behind this trick leads directly to the attention mechanism in the next piece.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: Seq2Seq = an encoder LSTM squeezes the whole sentence into an 8,000-dimensional vector + a decoder LSTM generates the translation word by word from that vector. It was the first end-to-end neural translation system and beat traditional statistical translation at scale. Its weakness is equally clear: no matter how long the sentence, all information has to fit into one fixed-length vector.

callout.title: Four small concepts for this piece
callout.text: You can get by with just these four:
list: **Word vectors**: Each word is represented by hundreds or thousands of numbers, and similar words have similar vectors. See the previous article in this thread, word2vec.
**Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)**: Read one word at a time; after each word, update a “memory” (hidden state), then read the next. They are naturally suited to sequences of variable length.
**LSTM**: An RNN with gates that decide what to remember and what to forget. It retains information from much earlier in the sequence better than a vanilla RNN.

**BLEU**: The most common automatic score for machine translation. It measures how many word n-grams overlap between the machine translation and human reference translations. It runs from 0 to 100; higher is better.

sections.h: The problem: neural networks can only handle fixed-size inputs and outputs

blocks.p: By 2014, deep neural networks were already achieving excellent results in speech recognition and image recognition. The paper opens with an example of their power: with only two hidden layers, they can sort N N-bit numbers. Given enough labeled data, backpropagation tends to find the right parameters.

But they have a fundamental limit: **inputs and outputs must be encoded as fixed-dimensional vectors**. An image can be scaled to a fixed size; a sentence cannot. Sentences to translate vary in length, the target length is unknown in advance, and word order can differ completely between languages. Speech recognition, machine translation, and question answering are all essentially one sequence becoming another, and at the time there was no general neural solution for such problems.

The best translation systems then were **phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT)** systems: cut a sentence into phrases, look them up in a huge phrase table, then use statistical models to reorder and choose the most fluent combination. They were assembled from many hand-designed components and worked well, but they were complex. Neural networks usually played only a supporting role, such as rescoring candidate translations produced by the SMT system.

callout.title: More like written translation than simultaneous interpreting
callout.text: A vanilla RNN is good at tasks where it reads one word and emits one word, with inputs and outputs aligned one-to-one, like word-by-word interpreting. But translation requires taking in the whole sentence, understanding the meaning, and reorganizing it in another language: English adjectives usually come before nouns, French often after; German verbs can move to the end of the sentence. Seq2Seq's logic is written translation: read first, then write.

sections.h: The model: one LSTM reads, another LSTM writes

blocks.p: The core idea is very direct: use one LSTM to read the input sentence word by word; when finished, its final hidden state is the sentence vector v. Then use another LSTM, initialized with v, to generate the output word by word like a language model until it emits the end-of-sentence token <EOS>.

fig.title: Seq2Seq in two stages: read the whole sentence into a vector, then write the translation from that vector
fig.subtitle: Illustrative; based on paper Figure 1 and Section 2. Input “A B C”, output “W X Y Z”.

steps.name: Encoder reads in
steps.desc: Reads C, B, A, <EOS> in (reversed) order, updating its memory after each word.

steps.name: Sentence vector v
steps.desc: The hidden state after the encoder finishes is the representation of the whole sentence. In this paper, that means 8,000 numbers.

steps.name: Decoder generates
steps.desc: Starting from v, generate W; feed W back as the next input to generate X; then Y and Z, until emitting <EOS>.

plain.title: One reads, one writes
plain.text: The first LSTM reads the entire source sentence (A B C), then compresses its understanding into a vector v (gold). The second LSTM takes v and writes the translation word by word (W X Y Z). That single vector is the only channel between them.

blocks.p: Expressed as probabilities, the model estimates: given an input sequence x_{1}, …, x_{T}, what is the probability of the output sequence y_{1}, …, y_{T'}? The two sequences may have different lengths.

parts.desc: The final hidden state after the encoder reads the whole input; a fixed-length representation of the entire sentence
The probability that the next word is y_{t}, given the sentence vector and the previous t − 1 generated words. It is computed with a softmax over 80,000 French words.
The product: the probability of the whole translation equals the product of the probabilities of the word chosen at each step.
End-of-sentence token. Every sentence ends with it, so the model can decide on its own when to stop and can produce sequences of any length.

formula.note: The decoder is essentially a language model conditioned on the input sentence: a normal language model predicts the next word from previous words, but this one also conditions on the source sentence vector v.

plain.title: The probability of the whole sentence is the product of the probabilities at each step.
plain.text: Writing the translation is like a word-chain game: at each step, using v and the words already written, guess the probability of the next word. The probability of the full translation is the product of those step-by-step probabilities. Nail each step and the whole sentence comes out right.

blocks.p: The paper makes three key changes to this basic framework:

list: **Two separate LSTMs**: The encoder and decoder have separate parameters. This almost doubles the parameter count at negligible computational cost and makes it natural to train on several language pairs at once.
**A four-layer LSTM**: Depth clearly beats shallower models; each extra layer lowers perplexity by nearly 10%. Perplexity measures how “surprised” the model is by the data; lower is better.
**Reverse the input sentence**: Instead of mapping a, b, c to α, β, γ, the model maps c, b, a to α, β, γ. This is the most unexpected change; the next section covers it.

callout.title: What the LSTM's gates are doing
callout.text: A vanilla RNN rewrites its entire memory after each word, so by the end of a sentence the information from the beginning has been diluted; during training, gradients also tend to vanish or explode across long distances. LSTM adds several learnable gates to the memory: the forget gate decides how much old memory to discard, the input gate decides how much new information to write, and the output gate decides how much to expose at the current step. Information that needs to be kept long-term can keep the gates closed and carry forward through many steps.

sections.h: The key trick: reverse the source sentence

blocks.p: The paper finds that reversing the words in the **source sentence** only—leaving the target unchanged—makes the LSTM learn much better: test perplexity drops from 5.8 to 4.7, and a single model's decoded BLEU rises from 25.9 to 30.6. The authors admit they lack a complete explanation, but they offer a convincing conjecture.

During training, source and target sentences are concatenated end to end. In normal order, the first word of the source sentence is separated from the first target word by the entire source sentence; gradients must travel that long distance to connect them. After reversal, the first source word becomes the last one read, sitting right next to the first target word. **The average distance between corresponding words is unchanged, but the shortest distance shrinks sharply.** The paper calls this the “minimal time lag.”

fig.title: Reversed input doesn't change the average distance, but it brings the opening words close together
fig.subtitle: Illustrative; computed for this piece. Source sentence a b c, target α β γ, with an <EOS> between them; distance means the number of steps from a source word to its corresponding target word.
columns: Normal order: a b c <EOS> α β γ
Reversed order: c b a <EOS> α β γ
fig.note: The longer the sentence, the bigger the effect: in a 10-word sentence, normal order puts every pair 11 steps apart; reversed order brings the shortest pair down to 2 steps while the average remains 11. Learn the opening word pairs first, and the later pairs become much easier.

plain.title: Read it backward and the first pair sits close
plain.text: In normal order (A), the source sentence's first word a encounters its translation α only after several steps. Reverse the source (B), and a sits right next to α. The average distance doesn't change, but now a few word pairs are very close. The model learns those first, and the later ones become much easier.

blocks.p: The authors initially expected reversal to make the beginning of the translation more accurate and the end worse. The opposite happened: LSTMs trained on reversed source sentences did much better on long sentences. They suspect that reversal lets the LSTM make better use of its memory.

callout.title: “LSTM has a good memory, so reversal shouldn't be necessary”
callout.text: In theory, an LSTM can represent long-range information, but being able to represent it is not the same as being easy to learn. Under stochastic gradient descent, long-range dependencies initially receive almost no useful gradient signal. Reversal gives the model a set of nearby handholds so it can first establish communication between source and target. The paper's conclusion puts it this way: find an encoding that creates as many short-range dependencies as possible.

quiz.q: When the input is reversed, what happens to the average distance between corresponding words in the source and target sentences?
options: It stays the same, but the shortest pairs become much closer.
quiz.why: Reversal is only a rearrangement: the opening word pairs get closer, the later pairs get farther apart, and the average is unchanged. The paper's explanation is that the key is not the average distance but the minimal time lag: with some very close pairs, gradients can establish source-target connections early.

blocks.p: The data is a selected subset of the WMT'14 English-French translation dataset: 12 million sentence pairs (348 million French words, 304 million English words). The vocabulary is fixed: 160,000 most frequent words for the source language English, 80,000 for the target language French, and every other word is replaced with UNK (unknown word).

The model is a 4-layer LSTM with 1,000 cells per layer and 1,000-dimensional word embeddings. Each layer has a 1,000-dimensional hidden state and a 1,000-dimensional memory cell, so across all 4 layers, **a sentence is represented by 8,000 numbers**. The 384 million parameters break down like this:

fig.title: Nearly 80% of the 384M parameters are vocabulary-related
fig.subtitle: Illustrative; computed from the paper's Section 3.4 configuration and matching the paper's total and recurrent-connection counts exactly.
fig.note: The paper says 64M of the 384M parameters are “pure recurrent connections”—32M in the encoder and 32M in the decoder—matching the gate-level calculation here. The LSTM circuitry that does the actual understanding and generation accounts for only about one-sixth.

blocks.p: Training details (paper Section 3.4):

list: Parameters are initialized uniformly at random between -0.08 and 0.08.
Stochastic gradient descent without momentum, with a fixed learning rate of 0.7. After 5 epochs, the learning rate is halved every half epoch, for a total of 7.5 epochs.
Batches of 128 sentences. To prevent exploding gradients, any gradient whose norm exceeds 5 is scaled down to 5.

Most sentences are only 20 to 30 words; a few exceed 100. Random batching wastes a lot of computation padding short sentences, so keeping all sentences in a batch similar in length roughly doubles the speed.

blocks.p: A single GPU processes only about 1,700 words per second, which is too slow. The paper uses an 8-GPU machine with model parallelism: each of the 4 LSTM layers runs on a different GPU and passes its results to the next layer as soon as they're ready; the remaining 4 GPUs split the 80,000-word softmax, each handling a 1,000 × 20,000 matrix. This reaches about 6,300 words per second, and training takes roughly 10 days.

quiz.q: The paper says the deep LSTM represents a sentence with 8,000 real numbers. Where does 8,000 come from?
quiz.why: Each LSTM layer keeps two vectors, the hidden state and the memory cell; both are 1,000-dimensional, and 4 layers total 8,000 numbers. Those 8,000 numbers are the entire message the encoder passes to the decoder. The 8 GPUs are just hardware and have nothing to do with the representation size.

sections.h: Decoding: beam search, and a very small beam is enough

blocks.p: After training, translating means finding the most probable translation: T̂ = arg max_{T} p(T | S). But the set of possible French sentences is far too large to enumerate, so the search is approximate. The paper uses **left-to-right beam search**: always keep only the B most promising partial translations, extend each with every possible next word at each step, then keep the B most probable resulting prefixes. A candidate is complete once <EOS> is appended.

fig.title: Why not choose the best word at every step: greedy search can miss a better full sentence
fig.subtitle: Illustrative; the probabilities are invented for this piece. Beam size B = 1 is greedy; B = 2 keeps one extra candidate.
fig.note: Greedy search picks the most probable first word, Le, and ends with 0.20 overall. With beam size 2, keeping both Le and La lets the search discover that La maison is better as a whole (0.27).

plain.title: Keep one extra candidate, and one wrong step doesn't doom the whole sentence
plain.text: At each step, choosing only the single most likely word—greedy search—picks Le first and ends with just 0.20 for the full sentence. Keeping one extra candidate (beam size 2) lets the model notice that the slightly worse first word La, followed by maison, actually yields a better whole sentence (0.27).

blocks.p: Interestingly, the paper finds the beam doesn't need to be large at all: beam size 1 (greedy) already works well, and size 2 captures most of the benefit. A 5-model ensemble with beam size 2 scores BLEU 34.50, just 0.3 below the 34.81 from beam size 12, at far lower cost.

The paper's training objective is also plain: maximize the average log probability of the correct translation over all training sentence pairs, 1/|S| · Σ log p(T | S). No translation rules, alignment tables, or reordering models—everything is learned from the data.

sections.h: Results: first to beat statistical machine translation at scale

fig.title: Direct translation: 5-model ensemble of reversed LSTMs reaches BLEU 34.81, beating the SMT baseline
fig.subtitle: WMT'14 English-to-French test set, from paper Table 1. Amber marks the best score.
rows: Bahdanau et al. (with attention; covered in the next close reading)
fig.note: An ensemble means five models that differ only in random initialization and minibatch order vote together. The 34.81 comes with a French vocabulary of only 80,000 words: whenever a reference translation contains an out-of-vocabulary word, the model necessarily loses points.

blocks.p: The paper emphasizes that this is **the first time a pure neural translation system has outperformed phrase-based statistical machine translation at scale by a clear margin**, and that the neural network has a limited vocabulary and was barely tuned, while the SMT system's vocabulary is effectively unlimited.

fig.title: Rescoring the SMT system's candidates: 36.5, just 0.5 shy of the best result at the time
fig.subtitle: WMT'14 English-to-French test set, from paper Table 2. Amber marks the best LSTM rescoring result.
rows: Cho et al. (RNN encoder-decoder + statistical machine translation)
Best WMT'14 result at the time
Oracle upper bound: always pick the best candidate
fig.note: For rescoring, the LSTM computes a log probability for each of the 1,000 candidates from the SMT system and takes an even average with the SMT system's own score.

blocks.p: **Long sentences didn't fall apart.** At the time, other researchers using similar architectures saw translation quality drop sharply on long sentences—the reason Bahdanau et al. introduced attention in the next paper. This model, however, handled long sentences well: after sorting by sentence length, sentences up to 35 words showed no degradation at all, and only the longest group declined slightly. The authors credit reversed input.

**The sentence vectors carry meaning.** Projecting encoded vectors for some phrases into two dimensions with PCA clusters sentences with similar meanings: “Mary admires John” and “Mary is in love with John” sit close together, while “John admires Mary” lands on the other side. This shows the vectors are sensitive to word order, not just a bag of words. Active and passive sentences (“She gave me a card in the garden” and “I was given a card by her in the garden”) fall nearby.

quiz.q: Why does the paper specifically point out that the 34.81 score was achieved while out-of-vocabulary words were penalized?
options: To explain why it didn't beat statistical machine translation.
To show the score is underestimated: the French vocabulary is only 80,000 words, the model can't output rare words from the reference translations, and there is plenty of room for improvement.
Because BLEU doesn't count out-of-vocabulary words.
Because statistical machine translation has the same limitation.
quiz.why: For out-of-vocabulary words, the model can output only UNK, which by definition cannot match the reference, so the score is conservative. The SMT system has no such vocabulary limit. The paper sees this as evidence that a relatively untuned, limited-vocabulary neural network has already beaten SMT, and that further improvements will do even better.

list: **Two numbers for the reversal gain don't match.** Section 3.3 says a single model's BLEU rises from 25.9 to 30.6, but the corresponding rows in Table 1 read 26.17 and 30.59. The former probably comes from a different setting or an earlier experiment; the paper doesn't say.

**“No difficulty on long sentences” is a bit strong.** The abstract says the LSTM had no difficulty with long sentences, but the caption of Figure 3 is more precise: no degradation up to 35 words, with a slight drop for the longest sentences.

**The BLEU script affects the conclusion.** The paper says it used the multi-bleu.pl script. With that same script, the best WMT'14 system scores 37.0, higher than the 35.8 reported on the official site. Different BLEU scripts can differ by more than a point, so comparisons across papers need extra care.

**It cites the next paper.** The main text already mentions Bahdanau et al.'s attention-based translation model and includes its 28.45 in Table 1. The two papers appeared at almost the same time; read the next one side by side with this one.

**The fixed-length bottleneck.** Whether the input is 5 words or 50, the encoder must squeeze it into the same 8,000 numbers. The longer the sentence, the more information is likely lost. Reversing the input eases optimization, but it doesn't remove the bottleneck.
**Limited vocabulary.** With an 80,000-word French vocabulary, rare words can only be emitted as UNK. Later subword segmentation, such as the BPE in this reading list, solves this.
**Slow.** LSTMs must compute word by word, training is hard to parallelize, and the 384M-parameter model took about 10 days on 8 GPUs.
**Only one language pair.** The paper believes the approach generalizes to other sequence problems, but it only tested English-to-French.

blocks.p: **What came next.** The paper's conclusion is remarkably prescient: a large, deep LSTM that makes almost no assumptions about the problem structure can beat carefully engineered task-specific systems if the data is sufficient. The encoder-decoder framework later showed up in summarization, dialogue, speech recognition, image captioning—nearly every task that maps one sequence to another.

But the fixed-length vector remained a bottleneck. The next piece, Bahdanau attention, changes the approach: each time the decoder generates a word, it looks back at all the words in the source sentence and decides which ones to focus on, instead of relying only on one compressed vector. Three years later, the Transformer went further and simply removed the LSTM, leaving only attention. Today's large language models are, in fact, the decoder half of the Transformer.
First author Ilya Sutskever later became a co-founder and chief scientist of OpenAI, where the GPT series was built.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: Why does the decoder need the <EOS> end-of-sentence token?
options: So the encoder knows when the sentence has been read.
So the model can decide on its own when to stop, and can output sentences of any length.
quiz.why: The decoder generates one word at a time, and without an “end” option it wouldn't know when to stop. By treating <EOS> as an ordinary word to predict, the model can assign probabilities to sentences of different lengths. The encoder-side <EOS> also matters, but this question is about the decoder. Out-of-vocabulary words use UNK.

quiz.q: If the source sentence grows from 10 words to 50 words, what happens to the size of Seq2Seq's sentence vector v?
options: It depends on the vocabulary size.
quiz.why: This is exactly Seq2Seq's core weakness: the length of v is fixed, so a longer sentence must be represented with the same number of numbers. The attention mechanism in the next piece exists to break this limitation.

blocks.p: After reading this piece, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why can't an ordinary deep neural network do translation directly?
What do the encoder and decoder each do? Where is the sentence vector v produced, and who receives it?
Why can p(y | x) be written as a product of per-step probabilities? What does <EOS> do?
Why does reversing the input help? What does “minimal time lag” mean?
Where do the 384M parameters go?
Why is beam search better than greedy? Why is beam size 2 enough?
Why is the 34.81 score considered an underestimate?
What problem does the fixed-length sentence vector cause? How does attention solve it?
